Architecture

Under the hood
Why each one lands where it does — mechanism, not anecdote.
Maths Olympiad
A proof is checkable. A verifiable reward permits reinforcement learning and search over many candidate reasoning
traces at inference time — deliberation, not one forward pass.
Analog clock
Vision transformers embed image patches. Telling the time needs precise angular discrimination between two hands
— exactly the fine geometric relation patch embedding blurs. There is no “measure this angle” primitive.
Protein structure
Multiple sequence alignment supplies co-evolutionary signal: residues that mutate together are likely in contact.
Evolution ran the experiment; the PDB is decades of curated ground truth. AlphaFold 3 is diffusion-based.
Folding laundry
Cloth has unbounded degrees of freedom, self-occludes, and is partially observed. No simulator transfers.
Demonstrations cannot be scraped — everyone is collected in real time by a person.
Driving
Operational design domain. Performance is bounded by the long tail, not the average — and rare events are both
thinnest in the data and the ones that matter.
Counting letters
Byte-pair encoding. Deferred — we open this one up in C3, after the break.

How we know — and why to distrust these numbers
Every figure in this session came from a benchmark. Benchmarks are themselves contested.
ClockBench · RLBench · OSWorld
Each measures a narrow, defined slice. RLBench's 89.4% is rigid objects at known poses, in simulation. The 12% is a real house. Same
field, incomparable conditions.
The bar exam claim was overstated
OpenAI reported ~90th percentile. Martínez (2024) found the comparison group was skewed toward repeat takers who had already failed.
Against first-time takers: ~62nd. Against those who passed: ~48th overall, ~15th on essays.
Benchmarks contain errors
A review found invalid-question rates from 2% on MMLU Math to 42% on GSM8K. Frontier models gained 30 points in one year on a
benchmark built to resist them — saturation, or contamination?
Sources: AI Index 2026 · Martínez, E. (2024), Artificial Intelligence and Law

Appendix — for the curious
Not part of the 26 minutes.
Why does a classifier beat a foundation model in its own lane?
It optimises a narrow decision boundary against your exact data distribution. A general model spends most of its capacity on things irrelevant
to your task. Specialisation wins when the task is fixed and the data is representative.
Isn't the API just a classifier underneath?
No. It is doing next-token prediction, and you are choosing to read the output token as if it were a label. A classifier returns a calibrated
probability for every class — 0.87 positive, 0.13 negative — so you can set a threshold and route anything below it to a human. The API
returns the word “positive”, with no honest confidence attached. In production that difference decides whether you can automate at all.
What is actually inside an embedding vector?
A few hundred to a couple of thousand numbers. No individual number means anything you could name — there is no “politeness” dimension.
What is meaningful is DISTANCE: the model was trained so that texts with similar meaning end up near each other. You are not reading the
vector, you are measuring how close it is to others. That is also why you cannot inspect one to explain a decision.

Three failures, one mechanism.
Cannot count letters
The word is 3 tokens, not 10 letters. Counting means recalling a property of an opaque

Cannot hit an exact word count
Same root, plus no lookahead. It commits to each token without a plan for the total.

Different mechanism, same shape. Vision models see image patches, not angles.

How a text predictor becomes an assistant
Three stages of training. Only the first is expensive.
PRETRAINING
10 TB of internet text
Millions of dollars.  Done rarely.
Makes it KNOWLEDGEABLE.
What comes out is a base model. It only continues documents — ask it a question and it may
reply with more questions, because that is what a page of questions looks like.
FINE-TUNING
~100,000 written conversations
Cheap.  Done often.
Makes it USEFUL.
Humans write ideal question-and-answer pairs. It learns the shape of being asked something and
answering. It is not learning new facts here — it is learning a format.
PREFERENCE TUNING
Humans ranking answers
Cheap.  Continuous.
Makes it AGREEABLE — and makes it refuse.
Ranking two answers is far easier than writing a perfect one, so you can gather a lot of it. This is
where politeness comes from. It is also where refusals come from.
→ Class 6
10 TB versus 100,000 conversations — five orders of magnitude.  Nearly everything it KNOWS came from stage 1. Nearly
everything about HOW IT BEHAVES came from 2 and 3.

So — why is the frontier jagged?
Two mechanisms. You have now seen both of them happen.
REPRESENTATION
The model only sees what the encoding left
behind.
Text becomes tokens. “strawberry” arrives as three ID numbers —
there are no letters anywhere in the system.
Images become patches. The fine angle between two clock hands
is blurred by the encoding.
Ask about information the encoding destroyed, and it can only
guess.
PREDICTABLE  — know the encoding, know the failure.
EMERGENCE
Capabilities arrive with scale, unannounced.
Multi-step arithmetic, reasoning step by step, learning from
examples inside the prompt — near-useless at small scale,
present at large.
Nobody could say in advance which would appear, or at what
size.
The only way to find out what a model can do is to try it.
NOT PREDICTABLE  — there is no rule. Only testing.
One half you can reason about. The other half you cannot — so you test it.  That is what A1 is for.
Neither is solved by scale alone.  The first needs a different encoding, or a tool that can count. The second does not get more
predictable as models grow — if anything, less.

From talking to doing
An agent is not a new kind of model. It is a model, plus tools, plus a loop.
The model emits a
special token
→
Surrounding code
intercepts it
→
The tool runs — search,
calculator, code
→
The result is fed back
into the context
→
The model continues,
now informed
It did not “decide” to use a tool.  Fine-tuning taught it when to emit that token, by example. Everything
agentic you have read about is this loop, wrapped in better engineering.
↳The token is a structured function call the runtime parses and executes. Nothing is autonomous — the loop is ordinary software calling a model repeatedly.
Errors compound across steps, which is why multi-step agents fail far more than single calls.

Inside the model: attention and the context window
What attention actually does
At every position the model computes how much each earlier token should influence the next prediction. Those weights are learned, not fixed —
which is how it handles “the animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired” and knows what “it” refers to. Before transformers, that
relationship had to travel step by step through a chain; attention lets any token look directly at any other in one operation.
Why the context window is a hard wall
Attention compares every token with every other, so cost grows roughly with the square of the length. Double the context, quadruple the work. That
is why context limits exist, why long documents cost disproportionately more, and why retrieval — fetching only the relevant passages — is usually
cheaper than pasting everything in.
What the parameters are not
There is no database inside. No lookup table, no facts stored in rows. Knowledge is distributed across billions of weights in a form nobody can read
directly. This is why you cannot patch a specific wrong fact, and why interpretability is an open research field rather than an engineering task.

Why the same prompt gives different answers
The most common confusion about these systems, and it has a simple cause.
The model does not output a word. It outputs a probability for every token in its vocabulary — often
100,000 of them.
Something then has to pick one. Always take the highest-probability token and the output is repetitive and flat. Sample from
the distribution instead and you get variety — and a different answer each time.
Temperature
Flattens or sharpens the distribution. Near 0 is near-deterministic and dull; higher is more varied and less
reliable.
Top-p / top-k
Restricts sampling to the most likely candidates, cutting off the improbable tail that produces nonsense.
What this means for you
An eval run once is not evidence. If you change a prompt and the output improves, that may be sampling,
not your prompt. Run it repeatedly — which is exactly what A1 Part 3 asks.

Per-call operating cost
Small individually. Paid on every single call, forever, and it
scales linearly with usage. This is the number that decides
whether your product works.

So — what is an agent?
DEFINITION
One definition from the reading — and the two things that must be true for it to hold.
The definition.  Anthropic, in Pre-read 1: an agent is a system where the model “dynamically directs its own processes
and tool usage, maintaining control over how it accomplishes tasks.”
In one line:  an agent decides its own next step, takes it, looks at what happened, and decides again — until it decides to
stop.
Two conditions — take either away and it is something else.  (1) The steps are not known in advance — the model
chooses them at runtime, so their number varies with the input. (2) It gets ground truth back at every step — a tool
result, a query, code that ran — so reality can correct it. Without (1): a workflow. Without (2): a monologue.
Three tasks, three answers:  “Translate this page” → one call. “Extract invoice fields, validate, post to the ledger” → a
workflow: the same three steps every time (opening quiz, Q1). “Find out why this shipment is late and get a new date” → an
agent: nobody can say how many steps that takes.
Everything after this slide is a consequence of those two conditions — the loop, the memory, the patterns, and the reasons it fails.
Takeaway   Two tests: the model picks the steps, and the world answers back. Both, or it is not an agent.

DEFINITION
Two different things share one word. Confusing them is how agent projects overspend.
Working memory — the transcript itself.  Every thought, action and observation so far, resent in full on each turn. It is
free to write and it is the reason a long run costs more per turn than a short one. It also degrades: as the window fills,
the model attends less well to any one thing in it — Anthropic calls this context rot.
In one line:  working memory is what the agent is holding.
Persistent memory — a store outside the run.  A notes file, a progress log, a database row, a vector store. The agent
reads it at the start and writes to it at the end, so tomorrow’s run knows what today’s did. This is the difference
between an assistant that resumes and a chat that ends.
In one line:  persistent memory is what the agent chose to keep — and, in a regulated setting, what you must be able to
explain.

contradict.
April 2026 — “Multi-agents: what’s actually working.”  Not a reversal, a narrowing: several agents may contribute
intelligence, but the writes stay single-threaded. What works — a review agent with clean context reading another
agent’s output (~2 bugs per pull request, 58% severe), and a cheap model escalating hard problems to a frontier one.
The rule to keep:  multiple minds, one hand on the keyboard.

When NOT to build an agent
THE HARD PART
Two tests. If a task fails either one, build the rung below instead.
1 · The ground-truth test.  Ask first: what will tell this loop it is wrong, and how fast? A failing test suite answers in
seconds and cannot be argued with; a customer’s satisfaction answers in days and is a matter of opinion. Fast and
objective → build the agent, wiring that signal in first. Slow or subjective → a workflow with a human gate.
And if there is no signal at all:  you do not have an AI problem, you have an unspecified one — no amount of autonomy fixes
an objective nobody can state.
2 · The arithmetic.  A step that works 95% of the time, run 20 times: 0.95²⁰ ≈ 0.36 — roughly a one-in-three chance of a
clean run. At 99% per step it is still only ≈ 0.82. Three ways out: raise per-step reliability (hardest), cut the number of
steps (biggest win), or make failure recoverable with gates, checkpoints and retries.
Which is why:  most of a good agent, by volume of code, is recovery machinery rather than intelligence.
Quiz question 6, in the opening — the number surprises almost everyone, including people who build these for a living. And autonomy is a dial, not a switch: suggest → confirm →
act. You set that dial in code after the break (Pre-read 5).
Takeaway   Autonomy without recovery scales badly. Fewer steps beats smarter steps.

FOR BUILDERS
The tool description is the entire manual — and the reader cannot ask you a question.
The agent–computer interface.  A human engineer reads your docs, hovers a tooltip, tries it in staging, and asks a
colleague. The model does none of those. It sees a name, a signature and a sentence, and then it commits.
So:  every ambiguity you leave is one it will resolve confidently, wrongly, and at scale. Write for a very capable colleague who

Four interface rules — Pre-read 1.  (1) Room to think: enough tokens to think “before it writes itself into a corner” —
generation runs left to right and a token cannot be retracted. (2) Familiar formats, close to what the model has seen in
ordinary text. (3) No bookkeeping — no counting, escaping or indentation.
Rule 4 is the next slide:  mistake-proof the tool instead of instructing the model.
The four sit under principle 3, the ACI. The other two: simplicity — every tool enters the menu, is re-billed every turn, and widens a surface you cannot test — and transparency, the
last chance to intervene before the irreversible step.

Guardrails live in code, not in the prompt
FOR BUILDERS
Two kinds. Bounds cap what the loop may spend. Gates stop it before the one act it cannot undo.
BOUNDS — three lines, no AI.  A step cap. A budget ceiling. Action dedupe. In the notebook these turn a silent eight-
turn burn into a loud stop at turn three, and recover 75% of the wasted spend on a single run.
Fail safe and loud:  the agent still fails — that is fine. What changes is that it now says why, in three turns instead of eight.
GATES — a dial, not a switch.  autonomy = suggest | confirm | act. And notice where the gate sits: in front of the one
tool that touches the world, not in front of the agent. The reads stay unsupervised because they are reversible.
Which is Capsule 1’s cliff, in code:  the governance line is not RAG → agentic RAG. It is the first write.
Two safeties in different layers: the gate asks at the moment of action; dry_run=True makes the safe state the default. Spark ships the same pair — it asks before spending your
money, permissions off by default (Pre-read 4).
Takeaway   Most of a good agent, by volume of code, is recovery machinery.

THE ENVELOPE
Nobody publishes what an agent costs to run. A price plus a usage cap is the closest public proxy we have.
Spark, in ten weeks.  US$249.99 a year earlier; US$100 at I/O in May 2026; on the US$20 Pro tier by 27 July. It is not on
the free tier — the first Google AI feature in years that could not be given away.
Two readings, and they predict different things:  inference got cheaper, or distribution was worth more than margin.
You cannot price a loop per seat.  Spark’s tiers differ by how much work the agent may do — roughly 5× and 20× the
Pro allowance — not by features. Cost scales with steps taken; revenue would have scaled with seats sold.
And the agent tier runs the fast model, not the biggest:  with many steps, cost and latency per step dominate.
The number you actually want is not cost per token, or even cost per task. It is cost per user per month at the 95th percentile — usage is Pareto-distributed, and an always-on agent
works overnight for the heaviest user (Class 3, AI Wars).
Takeaway   A usage cap is not a nicety. It is the only thing between a flat fee and an unbounded liability.

The third test is the bill:  does the value of one completed task exceed B×T + D×T²∕2, divided by how often the run works?

And a failed run is the cheap case:  in C2 the wrong answer cost less than the right one — and said it was done.
The denominator is not the success rate from your happy-path tasks. It is the one your negative cases gave you — which is why Capsule 2 spent time on them.

Two forces, pulling opposite ways
Most people know about the first one. The second is why the invoice went up anyway.
Force 1 — the price of a fixed capability collapses.  a16z: about 10× a year. GPT-3-quality output went from $60 per
million tokens in Nov 2021 to about $0.06 three years later — 1,000×. Stanford’s AI Index put GPT-3.5-level at $20.00 →
$0.07, over 280×.
The catch:  both are measured at FIXED capability. Nobody buys the 2021 capability.
Force 2 — the tokens a task consumes explode.  Reasoning models emit about 8× more tokens on the same questions,
with output length growing ~5× a year. Anthropic: agents ≈ 4× a chat, multi-agent ≈ 15×.
Energy says it too:  a short GPT-4o query ≈ 0.42 Wh; GPT-5 at high reasoning ≈ 17.15 Wh — about 40× for the same
question.
Takeaway   Price per token fell. Tokens per task rose. The third term is the one you choose.

There is no such thing as “AI failure”
Four kinds of AI, four different things we ask of them — and therefore four different errors.
What you ask for decides how it fails.  A classifier is asked for a LABEL, and a label is a compressed claim about a population. A

there by acting. An embodied system is asked for a MOVEMENT, and a movement changes the physical world.
So:  the failure mode is a property of the contract, not of the algorithm.
The control that catches one is silent on the others.  This is the practical consequence, and the reason the next twenty
minutes exist. A team that has built excellent monitoring is not protected against an irreversible action. A team with
excellent gates is not protected against a confident wrong answer.

Large language models — the fluent per-instance failure
NIST calls it CONFABULATION, and the word is better than hallucination.
HALLUCINATION.  The popular word, and the wrong picture. It implies a malfunction — a system perceiving something
that is not there. Nothing has malfunctioned.
CONFABULATION.  NIST AI 600-1’s term: the generation of confidently stated erroneous content. Borrowed from neurology,
where a patient produces a fluent, sincere, false account with no intent to deceive.
Which is why the second word is the right one: this is the system working.  A language model is trained to produce
text that is LIKELY. A fluent false statement and a fluent true statement are both likely. Correctness is not a variable the
model optimises, so it is not a variable the output reports on — and it does not hedge, slow down or lower its
confidence. A confabulated citation arrives in exactly the register of a real one.
For deployment:  you cannot detect a confabulation by reading it. The output carries no distress signal at all.
NIST AI 600-1 lists twelve generative-AI risks and confabulation is the second, after CBRN information — the list is alphabetical, not ranked.
Takeaway   Fluency and correctness come out of one mechanism. That is the whole problem, in one sentence.

Why SQL injection was solved and this was not
The contrast is where the insight sits. It is not that databases tried harder.
A database has a STRUCTURALLY separate channel.  Parameterised queries work because the engine parses the query
into a plan and then binds parameters as VALUES — two code paths, enforced below the application. A parameter
containing DROP TABLE is stored as a ten-character string, because the engine never re-parses it.
Result:  not reduced — ended, as a class of vulnerability, for anyone who uses them.
A transformer cannot tell one kind of token from another.  System prompt, user message and retrieved document
enter one sequence, and attention runs over them uniformly — no vector says where it came from. So every defence is
a convention the attacker can also write: delimiters (they write yours) · XML tags (they close yours) · “the following is
untrusted” (a sentence among sentences) · instruction hierarchies (a stronger prior — still a prior).
OWASP’s own text:  no reliable prevention mechanism exists today.
THE ASYMMETRY: in SQL the structure is fixed BEFORE untrusted input arrives. In an agent — which tools fire, in what order, with what arguments — it is decided AFTER, by the
same model that just read the input.
Takeaway   Assume the model can be convinced of anything, and design so that being convinced is survivable.

The role with no job title
It is the one about two thirds of this room is best placed for, and nobody advertises it.
Every team ends up with a translator.  They sit in finance, legal, clinical or operations — not in engineering — and they
are the one person who can tell whether the vendor is lying and what the thing will cost at volume.
You did not need to become technical for this.  You needed to know what questions survive contact with a confident
answer.
That person is scarce because the two halves rarely meet.  Technical people who understand the deployment context
are rare; domain people who understand what the model is doing are rarer. Building the small version yourself puts you
in the second.
Which is why:  you built a classifier, a RAG system and an agent, and you priced them per successful task — not to become
an engineer, but so that nobody can tell you a story about one.
Takeaway   You do not have to be the person who builds it to be the most useful person in the conversation.
